extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of sociology, criminology, race relations, and policing studies
extracted.subtask_short: analysis of moral panic and policing
extracted.subtask_description: Critically analyze how moral panics, media, official institutions and socio-economic conditions produced a 'law-and-order' response to street crime (the 'mugging' phenomenon) in 1970s Britain. Emphasises social-group positioning, state responses and the interplay of race and class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Displacement effect / moral-panic cycle
rubrics_metrics.description: The connection between the crisis and its appropriation in mass social experience passes through a series of false 'resolutions', primarily taking the shape of a succession of moral panics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An adequate account must show how surges of social anxiety are temporarily relieved by projecting fears onto compelling themes (discovery of demons, identification of folk-devils, moral campaigns, expiation via prosecution/control). None of these projections succeeds for long; the cycle repeats (e.g., Teddy Boys → mods and rockers → hooliganism → drugs / race / ghetto).

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence into a generalized threat ('general conspiracy')
rubrics_metrics.description: Particular moral panics converge and overlap so that diverse problems (sale of drugs, pornography, women's movement, critique of family) are experienced as facets of a single larger threat to the state and social order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how naming specific enemies is deceptive because the menace is presented as ubiquitous ('behind everything'), producing an abstract 'general conspiracy' that justifies far-reaching state responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition to 'law-and-order' society (suspension of liberties)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the threat is framed as subversion of the state from within, only a general exercise of authority and discipline — even at temporary expense of liberties — is deemed likely to succeed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis should identify mechanisms by which liberal protections are relaxed: rapid, forceful policing, surveillance, detention without charge, acting on suspicion, and other expanded powers; show ideological legitimation across political voices (populist, social-democratic, religious).

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on social-contextual explanation rather than individual motives
rubrics_metrics.description: The study aims to examine 'mugging' as a social phenomenon from the perspective of the society in which it occurs, not to reconstruct individual motives of muggers or victims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good explanations emphasize social position, group identity and structural factors rather than psychological reconstructions of offenders' motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish measurement/labeling effects from real changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Growth in 'mugging' may reflect two processes: (1) actual involvement of black youths in petty street crime, and (2) the assignment of the 'mugging' label to many petty crimes (snatchings, pickpocketing), producing a perception of 'mugging' as a 'black' crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accounts must disentangle statistical recording practices, labelling biases, and semantic extension of the term from genuine incidence increases; avoid treating headline figures as unqualified facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of media and official framing (double perspective)
rubrics_metrics.description: Media and official reports often deploy both a police-crime-control perspective and a social-problem (environmentalist) perspective simultaneously, with selective quotation amplifying dramatic figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should trace how press selection/quotations and official reports (e.g., Scotland Yard, Home Office) frame the issue, sometimes privileging sensational statistics over structural explanations, and how this framing fuels panic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of socio-economic and structural context (synchronisation of race and class)
rubrics_metrics.description: The economic recession, structural labour-market position of black youth, high unemployment, cuts in public expenditure and welfare all synchronized race and class aspects of the crisis, making policing blacks effectively policing the poor and unemployed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanations must incorporate macro-economic context, labour-market position, welfare retrenchment and how these interact with ethnic mobilisation to produce the policing problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official double strategy: containment via aid plus intensified policing
rubrics_metrics.description: The official response combined 'cooling' measures (expanded urban aid, community programmes, support for race-relations mediating agencies) with vigorous, intensified street policing in urban trouble-spots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good accounts should identify both remedial social programmes and coercive policing as complementary parts of state containment strategy, and assess contradictions and limits of this approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for politicisation and community mobilisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Black communities' responses became sharper, organised, collective and politicised (e.g., Brockwell Park incident mobilising adults, demonstrations, school strikes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include how grassroots mobilisation shifted legitimacy away from professional race-relations agencies toward activist black organisations and black press, affecting the dynamics of protest and policing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elite rhetoric, leaks and judicial pronouncements as panic accelerants
rubrics_metrics.description: Speeches by public figures (e.g., Powell), leaked reports (Foreign Office/Hawley) and judicial remarks (e.g., Judge Gwynn Morris) can precipitate or intensify public 'black panics'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse the causal role of elite discourse, leaks and courtroom statements in amplifying fear and legitimating harsher measures; track how officials' language reframes social problems as threats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extremist groups and scapegoating dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Organisations like the National Front exploited and amplified panic about 'mugging' and immigration, recruiting in working-class areas and promoting overtly racist, law-and-order messages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanations should consider how political entrepreneurs and fascist or xenophobic groups capitalize on moral panics, linking race, welfare and crime to mobilise support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data collection practices and operational recording (race recording)
rubrics_metrics.description: Police began recording race of victims and assailants 'for operational reasons', producing comparative statistics (e.g., '80% of attackers are black') that fed panics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how policing data practices, what is recorded and why, influence public perception; be alert to operational motives and potential biases in data compilation and release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic localisation and the 'ghetto' imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Mugging' and 'black crime' became tied to particular venues and localities (e.g., Brixton, Clapham), locating the problem geographically and ethnically in inner-city ghettos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good analyses show how naming places activates prior images of the 'ghetto' and situates crime as peculiar to those localities, reinforcing stigmatization and containment policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semantic evolution and racial connotation of crime labels ('return of the repressed')
rubrics_metrics.description: The label 'mugging', imported earlier with racial connotations, shifted over time from euphemistic handling to an explicit racialised identifier tied to black urban areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace how terms change connotation across phases (discrete uses, catch-all labels, racialised meanings) and how semantic shifts affect public understanding and policy responses.
